source: Changes to the feature values built from PanPhon, Hayes (2009) and the IPA vowel chart, each with the source that decides it.

overrides.source: Hayes (2009), Introductory Phonology, as converted to CSV by Gorman (github.com/kylebgorman/hayes2009, dataprep/Features.csv)
overrides.reason: Hayes gives the alveolar approximant no tongue-body value; PanPhon's [+high] describes the English bunched r, not the symbol.

overrides.source: Hayes (2009), Introductory Phonology, as converted to CSV by Gorman (github.com/kylebgorman/hayes2009, dataprep/Features.csv)
overrides.reason: Hayes gives [ɹ] [-round]; the IPA chart symbol carries no lip rounding.

diacritics.name: Centralized
diacritics.source: International Phonetic Association, The IPA Chart (revised to 2015), internationalphoneticassociation.org: the diacritic is named 'Centralized'
diacritics.reason: This table reads 'centralized' as a move to the central column of the chart, which is [-front, -back]. PanPhon's rule for it changes no feature.

diacritics.name: Advanced tongue root
diacritics.source: Casali (2007), 'Some observations on the phonetics of [ATR] contrasts', lecture, University of Education, Winneba (research.canil.ca/ATRLecture/Phonetics of ATR.pdf), section 2: [ATR] is an expansion or contraction of the pharyngeal cavity, after Lindau (1979), 'The feature expanded', Journal of Phonetics 7
diacritics.reason: PanPhon writes ATR as [+tense] and RTR as [-tense]. Here [tense] has no part in vowel height, and ATR is a contrast in the size of the pharyngeal cavity, so the mark sets [atr] and keeps [tense] as the base has it.

diacritics.name: Retracted tongue root
diacritics.source: Casali (2007), 'Some observations on the phonetics of [ATR] contrasts', lecture, University of Education, Winneba (research.canil.ca/ATRLecture/Phonetics of ATR.pdf), section 2: [ATR] is an expansion or contraction of the pharyngeal cavity, after Lindau (1979), 'The feature expanded', Journal of Phonetics 7
diacritics.reason: PanPhon writes ATR as [+tense] and RTR as [-tense]. Here [tense] has no part in vowel height, and ATR is a contrast in the size of the pharyngeal cavity, so the mark sets [atr] and keeps [tense] as the base has it.

diacritics.name: Palatalized
diacritics.source: Clements and Hume (1995), 'The internal organization of speech sounds', in Goldsmith (ed.), The Handbook of Phonological Theory, Blackwell, ch. 7, sections 3.5 and 3.5.1: a secondary articulation is a minor articulation linked under the C-place node beside the primary one
diacritics.reason: PanPhon writes the mark with the primary place features ['hi', 'back'], so it overwrote the base's place: in PanPhon kʲ and qʲ share a vector. The secondary articulation adds to the primary place and does not replace it, so the mark sets a feature of its own and the base keeps its place. The feature names are this table's.

diacritics.source: Clements and Hume (1995), 'The internal organization of speech sounds', in Goldsmith (ed.), The Handbook of Phonological Theory, Blackwell, ch. 7, sections 3.5 and 3.5.1: a secondary articulation is a minor articulation linked under the C-place node beside the primary one
diacritics.reason: PanPhon writes the mark with the primary place features ['hi', 'back', 'round'], so it overwrote the base's place: in PanPhon kʲ and qʲ share a vector. The secondary articulation adds to the primary place and does not replace it, so the mark sets a feature of its own and the base keeps its place. The feature names are this table's.

diacritics.name: Velarized or pharyngealized
diacritics.source: International Phonetic Association, The IPA Chart (revised to 2015), internationalphoneticassociation.org: the diacritic is named 'Velarized or pharyngealized'
diacritics.reason: The chart leaves the place open, so the mark sets both [velarized] and [pharyngealized] to 0: one of the two, not known which. The base keeps its place.

diacritics.name: Pharyngealized
diacritics.source: McCarthy (1994), 'The phonetics and phonology of Semitic pharyngeals', in Keating (ed.), Phonological Structure and Phonetic Form: Papers in Laboratory Phonology III, Cambridge University Press, pp. 218-219: the emphatics have 'a constriction in the upper pharynx' and 'should really be called uvularized'; Hermes, Barlaz, Shosted, Liang and Sutton (2017), Interspeech 2017, pp. 201-205; Al-Solami (2017), Canadian Acoustics 45(1), pp. 25-35: emphatics show 'tongue root and tongue dorsum retraction with inconsistent tongue root retraction'; Clements and Hume (1995), section 3.5: 'pharyngealization, involving the retraction of the tongue root'
diacritics.reason: PanPhon writes the mark as [+low, +back], which overwrote the base's place. Pharyngealized (emphatic) sounds constrict the upper pharynx with the tongue dorsum, at a different place from the pharyngeals (Hermes et al. 2017), and retract the tongue root inconsistently (Al-Solami 2017). The mark sets its own feature, [+pharyngealized], plus [-atr] for the tongue-root part, and keeps the base's place.

diacritics.name: Rhoticity
diacritics.source: International Phonetic Association, The IPA Chart (revised to 2015), internationalphoneticassociation.org: the diacritic is named 'Rhoticity'
diacritics.reason: PanPhon's rule gives [+high, +round, -anterior], so [ɚ] came out high and rounded. The chart names the mark only. This table reads it as a colouring that keeps the vowel's height and rounding, and keeps PanPhon's [-anterior].

diacritics.name: Voiceless
diacritics.source: International Phonetic Association, The IPA Chart (revised to 2015), internationalphoneticassociation.org: the diacritic is named 'Voiceless'
diacritics.reason: PanPhon applies the mark only to voiced sonorants, so [d̥] could not be read. It devoices any base.

diacritics.name: Voiced
diacritics.source: International Phonetic Association, The IPA Chart (revised to 2015), internationalphoneticassociation.org: the diacritic is named 'Voiced'
diacritics.reason: PanPhon has no rule for the mark. It voices any base.

diacritics.name: Raised
diacritics.source: International Phonetic Association, The IPA Chart (revised to 2015), internationalphoneticassociation.org: the diacritic is named 'Raised'
diacritics.reason: PanPhon's rule changes no feature. This table reads the mark as one chart row closer.

diacritics.source: International Phonetic Association, The IPA Chart (revised to 2015), internationalphoneticassociation.org: the diacritic is named 'Lowered'

diacritics.name: No audible release
diacritics.source: International Phonetic Association, The IPA Chart (revised to 2015), internationalphoneticassociation.org: the diacritic is named 'No audible release'
diacritics.reason: PanPhon has no rule for the mark. No feature of this table encodes release, so the mark is read and changes nothing.

diacritics.name: Half-long
diacritics.source: International Phonetic Association, The IPA Chart (revised to 2015), internationalphoneticassociation.org: the diacritic is named 'Half-long'
diacritics.reason: PanPhon has no rule for the mark. It sets [long] to 0, between short and long.

segments.name: voiced labiodental flap
segments.source: International Phonetic Association, The IPA Chart (revised to 2015), internationalphoneticassociation.org: pulmonic consonants, Tap or Flap row, Labiodental column
segments.reason: PanPhon does not list the symbol. It is a tap at the labiodental place: the manner of [ɾ] with the place of [v].

segments.name: voiceless epiglottal fricative
segments.source: Hassan, Esling, Moisik and Crevier-Buchman (2011), 'Aryepiglottic trilled variants of /ʕ, ħ/ in Iraqi Arabic', Proceedings of ICPhS XVII, Hong Kong, pp. 831-834: 'both pharyngeals and epiglottals occur at the aryepiglottic sphincter point of stricture', and sounds described as epiglottal 'are associated either with AE trilled varieties'; Esling (1996), 'Pharyngeal consonants and the aryepiglottic sphincter', Journal of the International Phonetic Association 26(2), pp. 65-88: the categories 'share a common place of articulation' and differ 'in manner of articulation'
segments.reason: PanPhon does not list the symbol. It is the pharyngeal fricative [ħ] made by the aryepiglottic folds, with trilling.

segments.name: voiced epiglottal fricative
segments.source: Hassan, Esling, Moisik and Crevier-Buchman (2011), 'Aryepiglottic trilled variants of /ʕ, ħ/ in Iraqi Arabic', Proceedings of ICPhS XVII, Hong Kong, pp. 831-834: 'both pharyngeals and epiglottals occur at the aryepiglottic sphincter point of stricture', and sounds described as epiglottal 'are associated either with AE trilled varieties'; Esling (1996), 'Pharyngeal consonants and the aryepiglottic sphincter', Journal of the International Phonetic Association 26(2), pp. 65-88: the categories 'share a common place of articulation' and differ 'in manner of articulation'
segments.reason: PanPhon does not list the symbol. It is the voiced counterpart of [ʜ].

segments.name: epiglottal plosive
segments.source: Hassan, Esling, Moisik and Crevier-Buchman (2011), 'Aryepiglottic trilled variants of /ʕ, ħ/ in Iraqi Arabic', Proceedings of ICPhS XVII, Hong Kong, pp. 831-834: 'both pharyngeals and epiglottals occur at the aryepiglottic sphincter point of stricture', and sounds described as epiglottal 'are associated either with AE trilled varieties'; Esling (1996), 'Pharyngeal consonants and the aryepiglottic sphincter', Journal of the International Phonetic Association 26(2), pp. 65-88: the categories 'share a common place of articulation' and differ 'in manner of articulation'
segments.reason: PanPhon does not list the symbol. The chart lists it under Other Symbols as 'Epiglottal plosive'. It is built as a voiceless stop at the pharyngeal place.
